analysis.one_liner: Requires internet providers to get customer consent before selling or sharing sensitive personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referral, as the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FCC to write rules requiring internet providers and phone companies to tell customers what data they collect, get explicit permission before using or selling sensitive information like browsing history, precise location, health and financial details, and to notify customers of data breaches. It also barred providers from cutting off service to customers who refused to consent. The bill never moved past its first committee referral; no hearing or vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of internet and phone companies, who today often have no practical say over whether their browsing history, app use, precise location, and other sensitive data is collected, used, or shared with advertisers and data brokers. The bill would have put the choice in the customer's hands: providers could only use sensitive data after affirmative, express consent, and they could not refuse service to customers who said no.

how_it_helps.text: Providers would have had to notify customers at the point of sale about what data is collected, how it is used and shared, and with whom, and to update customers when privacy policies change materially [S2] [S3].

Providers would have needed opt-in approval — affirmative express consent — before using or sharing sensitive information, including financial data, health data, children's information, Social Security numbers, precise location, content of communications, call records, and web browsing and app usage history [S2] [S3].
Providers could not have refused to serve customers who declined to consent to commercial use of their data, blocking 'take-it-or-leave-it' offers [S2] [S3].

Providers would have had to develop reasonable data security practices, notify customers of breaches, and the FCC would have had to prevent re-identification of supposedly de-identified data [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications and broadband carriers — the Comcast, AT&T, and Verizon class of companies — which would lose the ability to freely monetize customers' browsing history, location, and other sensitive data, and would bear the cost of new consent, notification, and security systems. Some of those costs could be passed to customers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The rules would cover only broadband, telecom, and VoIP carriers, not large web companies like Google and Facebook that collect similar data — critics of ISP-only privacy rules argue this creates uneven rules on who can use customer data [S2] [S3].

Compliance would cost carriers real money for consent-tracking, notification, and security systems, and some of that cost would likely show up in bills; opt-in rules could also constrain advertising-supported service pricing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary customers the benefits are direct and personal: control over browsing history, location, and sensitive financial and health data held by the companies they pay for internet access. The main cost is compliance spending by carriers and possible price effects, and the main design gap is that it leaves web giants unregulated. On balance the bill would have shifted power over personal data from companies to the people who generate it.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 11, 2017, by Rep. Keith Ellison with six original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1] [S3].
On July 14, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill gathered 10 cosponsors, all Democrats, before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4].

The bill arrived months after Congress and the President repealed the FCC's 2016 broadband privacy rules, which had required similar opt-in consent for sensitive data; this bill was an attempt to put such protections into law, and the committee never took it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband and telecom carriers are better off: without the bill, they kept the ability to collect and monetize customers' sensitive data without opt-in consent, since the FCC privacy rules had been repealed in 2017 and no replacement was ever enacted.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-led Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on the bill, and no Republican supported it [S3] [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required opt-in consent before carriers use or share sensitive customer data like browsing history and precise location, ending their ability to monetize that data by default; carriers benefit from the status quo where customers' data use is bundled into service agreements.
Carriers' data feeds targeted advertising; restricting its collection and sharing upstream would reduce the supply of precise location and browsing data available to ad networks and brokers.
